appraisal_events.evidence: son intelligence... avait pris un brillant que je ne lui avais jamais vu... il était comme un successeur... de M. de Charlus... il était aussi affable et charmant de caractère que l'autre était soupçonneux et jaloux.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator marks a striking growth in Saint-Loup's intellectual brilliance and wit, casting him as heir to Charlus's gift for talk while surpassing him in warmth and affability.

appraisal_events.evidence: elle résumait maintenant cette condamnation... en disant qu'il était «avant-guerre»... «Il ne voit personne, personne ne le reçoit», disait-elle à M. Bontemps... «Mais non, il est Prussien, disait la Patronne... membre héréditaire de la Chambre des Seigneurs de Prusse»... «Rien ne m'enlèvera de l'idée que pendant deux ans Charlus n'a pas cessé d'espionner chez moi.»
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme Verdurin wages a sustained, largely fabricated smear campaign against Charlus, calling him outdated, socially irrelevant, German, and a spy, and persuades impressionable listeners even as the narrator signals her account is self-serving and unreliable.

appraisal_events.evidence: ils étaient ingrats, car M. de Charlus était en quelque sorte leur poète, celui qui avait su dégager dans la mondanité ambiante une sorte de poésie... les gens du monde s'étaient désengoués de M. de Charlus, non pas pour avoir trop pénétré, mais sans avoir pénétré jamais sa rare valeur intellectuelle.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator explicitly defends Charlus's real distinction, arguing society is ungrateful and has never actually grasped the intellectual and poetic value it now dismisses as passé.

appraisal_events.evidence: de petites chroniques, transparentes pour ce qu'on appelait les initiés, avaient commencé à faire le plus grand tort à M. de Charlus... «Frau Bosch», «Frau von den Bosch» étaient les surnoms habituels... c'était non seulement cruel de la part de Morel, mais doublement coupable, car... il avait connu de lui... sa profonde bonté.
appraisal_events.explanation: Morel, who owed Charlus generous and delicate kindness, publishes coded, mocking chronicles branding him with German nicknames and doing him serious reputational harm, an act the narrator explicitly condemns as doubly culpable ingratitude.

status_effects.explanation: His intellectual brilliance and charm mark a clear rise in the narrator's estimation.
Once a celebrated fixture of society, he is now publicly recast by Mme Verdurin's campaign as outmoded, suspect, and possibly a German spy, and the world at large accepts the 'avant-guerre' verdict.
The narrator privately affirms Charlus's genuine intellectual and poetic worth even as his public standing collapses, a distinct movement from the social verdict against him.
Morel's published chronicles compound the public damage to Charlus's reputation with coded mockery of his nationality and inversion, a separate blow from Mme Verdurin's oral campaign.
The narrator condemns Morel as doubly culpable: he personally received Charlus's profound kindness yet turns to mock and defame him in print out of implacable hatred.

ambiguities: Mme Verdurin's claims that Charlus is German and a spy are reported with clear narratorial skepticism (she 'persuadait aisément' the credulous), so the social discredit is recorded as a witnessed social fact rather than an narrator-endorsed truth.
